editorials.title: Visits set stage for a weighty season of diplomatic dialogues
editorials.passage: A season of consequential diplomacy appears to be on hand as signals emerge from several directions at once. The unannounced visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, where he held talks with Russian intelligence officials is perhaps the brightest flare. The Kremlin confirmed the meetings while noting that Ratcliffe did not meet President Vladimir Putin. That distinction may be less important than the visit itself. At a time when US-Russia relations remain deeply strained, the fact that the CIA chief travelled to Moscow is significant. As the Kremlin noted, intelligence channels often remain open even during the darkest phases of diplomacy. India, meanwhile, is moving on multiple diplomatic tracks. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar’s visit to Moscow included a meeting with Putin and the delivery of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s personal message. More significantly, Jaishankar said Modi looks forward to meeting Putin at the forthcoming Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan this month-end and to welcoming him to India for the BRICS summit soon after.Then there is the China channel. National Security Adviser Ajit Doval’s talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi focused on border issues and the broader bilateral relationship. Beijing described the discussions as comprehensive, candid and friendly, while both sides announced steps to manage the border more effectively as they work towards a political solution..Coming ahead of a likely visit by President Xi Jinping—and amid continuing efforts to stabilise India-China relations after years of border tensions—the timing is difficult to ignore. Taken together, these developments suggest that the diplomatic calendar is indeed becoming consequential.The forthcoming SCO and BRICS summits offer platforms where countries that may disagree sharply on major geopolitical questions can still meet, talk, test possibilities and build consensus. In a fragmented international system, simply keeping these channels open matters.For India, this is a particularly important. New Delhi has consistently pursued strategic autonomy maintaining strong ties with Washington and Moscow while simultaneously managing a difficult but important relationship with Beijing. And across the Global South, countries are asserting greater agency in shaping a more diverse and genuinely multipolar international order.Amid this change, the willingness to talk creates space for de-escalation and greater understanding. Dialogue creates possibilities that confrontation cannot. editorials.title: Law imperils green cover in Garden City Bengaluru
editorials.passage: Bengaluru's civil society’s efforts to protect the city’s two lungs—Lalbagh and Cubbon Park, spread over 200 acres each—appear to be undermined with the passing of the Karnataka Government Parks (Preservation) Amendment Bill. It empowers the government to ‘alienate’ 5 percent of land in public parks for infrastructure projects in ‘public interest’, allowing the authorities to lease, sell, gift, exchange, mortgage or transfer the carved out land, though only to government departments and statutory bodies. The Bill was passed without debate while the opposition was busy creating a ruckus for the resignation of minister B Nagendra over a scam; the BJP and JDS are now denouncing it as serving the Congress government’s real estate interests. There was no such provision under the Karnataka Parks, Playfields and Open Spaces (Preservation and Regulation) Act, 1985.The amendment’s timing raises questions. It could pave the way for takeover of land in Lalbagh—six acres temporarily and one acre permanently—for Chief Minister D K Shivakumar’s pet tunnel project. The 17-km tunnel connecting Hebbal in north Bengaluru to Silk Board in the south will cut through Lalbagh. This has raised the hackles of ecologists, who have been demanding an environmental impact study before the project is finalised. Their main concern is how tunnelling will impact Lalbagh rock, a 3.4-billion-year-old peninsular gneiss formation that has been declared a National Geological Monument, apart from the loss of tree cover. The government claims the road will bypass the rock. .The project has been challenged in the Karnataka High Court for violating the Government Parks (Preservation) Act; the amendment circumvents any debate in court. While checks are in place by way of assessments by official committees, the change opens up space for misuse. It is also risking parks across the state and opening the gates for further loss of green cover—the state capital’s cover has plunged from 70 percent in the 1970s to 3 percent. For the government, 5 percent of Cubbon Park or Lalbagh would mean 10 acres at its disposal. It’s earlier attempt to put up a 10-storey structure in Cubbon Park was averted by alert citizens. editorials.title: Quick Take | Himalayan fury
editorials.passage: There’s no denying that the image of a massive body of water rushing to find level—like the videos that emerged from northern Nepal’s Rasuwa area on Wednesday—terrifies us. The flash flood pummelling down the Bhote Koshi river north of Kathmandu, triggered by an earthquake that set off an avalanche, has claimed at least 95 lives, with 600 others including 105 Indian nationals reported missing. While the government rushes relief to the neighbouring country, we must also look closer at the continuing flood devastation in Assam, where the Brahmaputra’s level is expected to rise again. With at least 107 deaths and 1.5 lakh people displaced, it’s a matter deserving national attention. editorials.title: A waiting economy
editorials.passage:
The youth protest brought attention to India’s job situation and to a by-now familiar statistic: around 40% of graduates aged between 15-25 years are unemployed. The number is alarming. The demonstrations that spread across the country and converged in New Delhi began with anger over examination irregularities and accountability demands over such leakages. But underneath these grievances lies a larger economic problem: millions of young Indians are spending some of their most productive years preparing, applying, waiting and trying again for a limited number of entries into secure employment. This economic phenomenon, visible in the protests, precedes the jobs question. It is a relatively less-discussed cost to the economy in terms of lost productivity and foregone output. There is little we know about the economic cost of this waiting or waithood , to put it succinctly.

India’s examination pipeline — the gateway to a decent work life — takes away some of the most productive years of a generation. Young persons preparing for a competitive examination — NEET, CUET, JEE, UPSC or any other — do not seem unemployed in the conventional sense. They may be studying, enrolled in coaching, taking exams, or filling out applications. Or they may be waiting for a result, a recruitment notification, a court decision or another attempt.

In economic terms, much of this is time spent outside productive employment. This time out has an opportunity cost. Graduates who spend two-three additional years preparing for a government job or professional entrance exams usually earn little or nothing. They are neither gaining work experience, nor acquiring any job-specific skill. They remain financially dependent on their families and delay decisions that typically follow stable employment — the first steps towards an independent life like moving out, buying or renting a home, forming a household, marrying, or simply becoming financially independent. This cost is not only borne by the graduates but also by the households that support them. And ultimately, it is borne by the economy that has invested in their education but is not fully exploiting their productive capacity.

This is the hidden economic cost of making young people wait. Indian households now finance this waithood at a gigantic scale, roughly equivalent to the test-preparation market that by now is a mid-sized industry — valued somewhere between $12-$15 billion and 9%-15% growth on a compounded annual basis — according to different estimates. JEE and NEET together account for nearly 70% of the undergraduate entrance-exam expenditure, which directly devolves upon individual households. This is not discretionary spending but indicates that the money that households would otherwise save or spend on other goods and services or finance the economic mobility the exam itself is meant to deliver but which, instead, is being staked repeatedly against narrowing odds.

The competitive exam system has thus become a labour market queue. Delayed entry into the workforce does not merely postpone earnings: it permanently lowers them. This is the least understood and examined cost of India’s waiting economy. The economist, Kunal Mangal, provides some remarkably clean evidence with his study of a partial, public-sector recruitment freeze in Tamil Nadu between 2001 and 2006. The pause on a subset of government jobs made the remaining vacancies more competitive. Aspirants, however, responded exactly as they do today — worked less to prepare more. A decade later, the affected set of people had lower employment rates, had delayed forming their own households, and displayed lower earning capacity compared to those candidates who had not faced the freeze, while the older family members compensated by extending their own retirement. This finding is an eye-opener and mirrors the broad trend amongst people who enter the workforce late or during a downturn — it is explained by the fact that earlier years in a career have the steepest wage growth in the work-life cycle. So losing out on these years does not just postpone earnings but permanently lowers them. A candidate who enters the workforce at 27 instead of 22 is not only five years behind but also may never fully catch up, according to research evidence.

The broader economic implication is that the real cost is not private. It is macroeconomic — and it is not visible. This is what makes the youth protests a genuine economic story, not just a social one. If even a fraction of India’s exam-aspirant segment — possibly several million people at any given time if we added together the UPSC, JEE, NEET, SSC, banking and state-service streams amongst important ones — were to enter the productive workforce, let’s say the private sector, two to three years earlier than they do at present, the gains would show up in every macroeconomic channel — for example, additional years of formal-sector output, additional consumption, additional direct-tax revenue (giving a much-needed boost to the country’s tax base) and, most important of all, additional human-capital accumulation of the right kind, such as on-the-job skills that are highly valued.

Do we know the aggregate costs of waiting in the labour market queue? A meaningful quantification is not known of at this point. However, even conservative, back-of-the-envelope calculations would place the annual output foregone as a result of queuing at a significant portion of total GDP. It is a figure worthy of official scrutiny for comprehensive understanding and policy formulation. A cost that is presumably large should not stay uncalculated. At present, the cost to the economy is invisible — someone in year three of NEET coaching is not counted as unemployed and is often not clearly categorised as ‘in education’ either; labour force surveys have no clean ‘aspirant’ group.

There is no doubt that the youth protests have shown that India’s growth model is not creating enough jobs. However, a more tractable problem occurs earlier in the pipeline. Unlimited attempts, decade-wide age windows, and artificially scarce seats fail to resolve the jobs shortage and, instead, actively manufacture a second one much before any job is at stake. That is a self-inflicted policy design problem, not of the business cycle and, unlike the job scarcity, is more easily addressed than the efforts required to increase the employment-intensity of India’s growth.

Renu Kohli is Senior Fellow, Centre for Social and Economic Progress, New Delhi. Views are personal

editorials.title: Careless whispers as capital
editorials.passage:
Miryam, if social media and some international newspapers are to be believed, is now a rich woman. In Colombia, where, according to some estimates, the average monthly income of women varies between 400 and 430 US dollars, Miryam — she hails from the agrarian province of Armenia — is today the proud owner of two mansions. But more than Miryam’s wealth, it is her path to prosperity that has shone the spotlight on her. Miryam did not strike gold, or oil. Her capital, interestingly, is chisme — gossip in Spanish. The lady monetises the information she gathers — Miss Marple-like? — her ears perpetually pricked at bits of buzz being churned out in her neighbourhood. Her methodology also involves teasing nuggets out of unsuspecting loose tongues during board games or in social gatherings. This ‘data’ are recorded diligently — in notebooks — and are tested for veracity: Miryam’s house apparently has a bulletin board bearing evidence in the form of photographs and notes. The price of information varies. The benign ones sell for, if the claims are to believed, between 5,000 and 10,000 pesos. But a sensitive matter, such as adultery, can pinch the client’s pocket. Miryam has said that she had once earned 700,000 pesos trading tittle-tattle for one such indiscretion.

Miryam has been praised for her business acumen; she has also been criticised for being an unethical busy­body. This inflamed debate, however, misses a larger point. Miryam’s ‘accomplishment’ should serve as an occasion to revisit the fascinating etymological, social, economic and cultural underpinnings of gossip.

Gossip’s antecedents can be traced back to the earliest epochs of recorded history. In Scandal: A Scurrilous History of Gossip , Roger Wilkes informs readers of a cuneiform Mesopotamian tablet from 1500 BCE whispering about a mayor’s affair with a married woman. But in medieval England, as Silvia Federici has pointed out in her work, Witches, Witch-hunting, and Women , gossip was synonymous with female companionship and solidarity, indicative of collective labour and its resultant emotional bonds among women. One of the sources that Federici cites as evidence of gossip’s glue in creating guilds of self-assertive women is a satirical — hilarious — mystery play of the Chester Cycle in which Noah’s wife refuses to leave with her husband even as the waters rise around them “unless she is allowed to take her gossips with her”. In the physical altercation that follows, Noah is beaten to a pulp by his formidable Missus. But by the 16th century, under a ferocious pushback against women’s autonomy by patriarchy and complicit institutions, such as the church, the meaning of gossip, Federici notes, had begun to get transformed — distorted — to indicate idle, amoral banter.

Yet science disproves gossip’s supposed gendered skin. Researchers from the University of California, Riverside had once made 467 adults, men and women, wear electronic recorders over a few days and, then, analysed the content of their conversations during that time period. The findings, which were published in Social Psychological and Personality Science , a peer-reviewed journal, revealed that not only had the majority of respondents of both genders indulged in gossip but also women, not men, had participated in gupshup that was ‘neutral’ — benign in research parlance.

Gossip gave Miryam an economic lifeline. But can chitchat serve as capital for altruistic, as opposed to personal, gain? The data on gossip as a force for collective economic well-being are revealing. Consider the set of experiments conducted by Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, Arun G. Chandrasekhar and Matthew O. Jackson in Karnataka and Haryana, respectively, the outcomes of which were published in The Review of Economic Studies . Broadly speaking, their findings suggest that gossip can function as a critical node for disseminating information to meet welfare goals: villages that could identify effective transmitters of important information, their experiment revealed, registered better vaccination rates among children.

And those who use the pulpit of the media to denounce prattle would perhaps do well to remember the productive relationship between the media and rumour mills. Roger Wilkes demonstrates how gossip’s potential, albeit as a moralising tool, coincided with the explosion of print culture. Indeed, the sensational divorce of Lady Colin Campbell — George Bernard Shaw’s muse — may not have taken place had it not been for a salacious newspaper article that fanned the flames. This combustible partnership between the media and hearsay was to be cemented in the years to come in the form of gossip and celebrity columns. Television and, now, digital media have been worthy successors in this regard. Literature’s fraternising with gossip is of note too. The content of Gertrude Stein’s The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas , an exposition on — exposé of — the avant-garde ambience in Paris, has been described by critics as nothing but fruity gossip about literary and art titans. But literature and art have also shown that prurience need not be gossip’s only moorings: its uses as a form of social commentary are not to be undermined. There are handy examples of this from domestic shores: Kaliprasanna Singha’s imaginative use of banter from Calcutta’s streets to reveal, among other things, the hollow pomposity and the pettiness of the affluent as well as rising class tensions in Hutom Pnyachar Naksha is one obvious example; Kalighat pats are another.

This is not to suggest that gossip is foolproof ethically. Its power and its perversity stem from a shared grey area: the fruition of targeted, toxic tidbits requires the absence of the defendant and an unprejudiced adjudicator. In other words, the non-availability of an instrument of authenticity, of truth — the foundational principle of jurisprudence — is a precondition for gossip’s survival and evolution. Gossip’s modern avatars, spread with lightning speed by social media platforms and algorithm-fed technology in post-truth polities, remain equally dependent on such an absence, indeed weakening, of cultures of accuracy, credibility and, above all, truth-telling.

Where does all this leave Miryam?

She may be a successful entrepreneur; she may be unethical. But mostly, the lady is a mirror, reflecting humanity’s meandering engagement with careless whispers.

editorials.title: Tricky balance
editorials.passage:
India will host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi next month under India’s presidency. BRICS has become central to the contest over the future of the international order. India’s approach has been a balancing act: strengthening the voice of the Global South without allowing BRICS to become an explicitly anti-Western coalition. The theme of India’s presidency — “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability” — captures this ambition. The emphasis on a “humanity-first” agenda intends to make BRICS an instrument of practical economic cooperation rather than an arena for geopolitical polarisation.

Disruptions, from the pandemic and supply-chain shocks to sanctions and geopolitical conflicts, have underscored the vulnerabilities of emerging economies. India is thus likely to push for more diversified and shock-resistant supply chains, particularly in critical minerals, agriculture, energy, and manufacturing. Innovation and digital integration provide another area where India has considerable diplomatic capital to deploy, especially its experience with Digital Public Infrastructure. The third pillar, cooperation, is inseparable from India’s longstanding advocacy of reformed multilateralism. New Delhi has long argued that institutions such as the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund, and World Bank no longer reflect the distribution of global economic and political power. BRICS gives India a platform to press for greater representation and agency for the Global South.

India seeks a more representative and responsive system while retaining an open, rules-based international framework. This distinguishes New Delhi’s approach from members that may view BRICS as a challenge to Western dominance. The trick for India will be to maintain its reformist orientation amid the divergent political preferences of an increasingly heterogeneous membership.

Several outcomes could give India’s agenda greater credibility. BRICS members could seek to expand local-currency trade and payment mechanisms, reducing transaction costs and de­pendence on third-country financial infrastructu­re. The New Deve­lopment Bank could play a larger role through increased local-currency lending for infrastructure and sustainable development projects. Supply-chain cooperation may prove particularly consequential. Coordination on critical minerals, food production, energy security, and manufacturing could move BRICS beyond declaratory diplomacy. Yet translating these ambitions into common policy will be difficult.

The principal challenge is that BRICS is not a strategically coherent bloc. Its members differ sharply — Russia and Iran, for instance, have an adversarial relationship with the West. New Delhi will thus have to resist pressures to turn BRICS into an explicitly anti-West platform while preserving its credibility within the group. The China question is even more complicated. India and China can cooperate on questions of Global South representation and economic reform while remaining strategic competitors. The durability of India’s BRICS diplomacy will depend, in part, on its ability to compartmentalise these competing interests.

The expansion of BRICS adds to the complexity. A larger membership enhances the grouping’s representational weight but makes consensus harder. Recent tensions between Iran and the United Arab Emirates are a case in point. Their opposing positions during the escalating regional confrontation contributed to divisions at the May BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in New Delhi, which ended without a joint communiqué. This presents a particular challenge for India because it has important strategic and economic interests in maintaining productive relations with both Tehran and Abu Dhabi. India will have to ensure that intra-group conflicts do not turn BRICS into an arena for the projection of regional rivalries.

India’s fourth BRICS presidency is thus significant for New Delhi to demonstrate that strategic autonomy remains compatible with effective multilateralism. The success of the 2026 presidency will depend on whether India can convert BRICS from a forum of divergent geopolitical interests into a platform for concrete cooperation and, in doing so, give substance to its claim to speak for a more representative Global South.

Harsh V. Pant is Vice-President for Studies and Foreign Policy, Observer Research Foundation

editorials.title: Mind the gap: Editorial on India’s education and jobs crisis
editorials.passage:
NITI Aayog’s latest findings indicate a waste of India’s demographic dividend. Unemployment among India’s graduates is four times the national average of 3.2% — 13% overall and an even higher 20.4% for women. Worse, only 8.25% of graduates get jobs aligned to their qualifications. More than half of employed graduates are concentrated in elementary or semi-skilled occupations. This exposes not only a grave failure in creating sufficient skilled employment but also shortcomings in higher education. Data show that the curricula of bachelor’s courses remain generic, theoretical, outdated and poorly connected to employment. Around 80% of higher-education students cite inadequate practical experience and industry exposure while 47% of formal workers identify the absence of internships as a major obstacle to finding work. Even those who do manage to find work suffer. Graduates without supplementary training earn an average starting salary of Rs 22,000 a month against Rs 29,000 for those with additional skills. A sizeable number of students who want to become entrepreneurs have no idea how to go about it. The scale of the crisis is evident in the widespread youth protests which may have electoral implications.

Educational challenges, though, are just one aspect of the problem. The shortage of skilled jobs is equally severe. India still employs 43% of its workers in agriculture and barely 12.1% in manufacturing. Recent employment growth remains heavily dependent on self-employment and unpaid family labour. There is also a paucity of private investment in job creation; this is important since public-sector recruitment alone cannot absorb India’s growing workforce. Ameliorative steps are necessary. Can China serve as a useful template, especially in education? Between 2021 and 2025, its universities closed or suspended 12,200 undergraduate programmes, introduced 10,200 and revised more than 30% of programmes, while its vocational-education law formally embedded apprenticeships and enterprise participation. The NITI Aayog report has underlined some reforms. India needs regular curriculum audits, published course-level placement and wage records, paid apprenticeships with enforceable standards, well-equipped public colleges, trained vocational teachers and industry partnerships tied to measurable employment outcomes. These reforms must accompany the creation of labour-intensive manufacturing jobs and skilling upgrades. Expanded care services and safe transport for women can help address the gender gap in skilled employment. But none of this will bear fruit unless economic policy creates enough secure and adequately paid work.

editorials.title: Rusted edge: Editorial on the limits of US sanctions against Iran
editorials.passage:
The United States of America has launched its latest economic sanctions targeting Iran and a set of individuals and companies that trade with it as part of Donald Trump’s pressure campaign against Tehran. Mr Trump’s administration has described the moves as an “Economic D-Day” for Tehran, effectively threatening to crush the Iranian economy, at a time when the US’s military campaign is yet to succeed in winning a war that Washington started — unprovoked — six months ago. But even in the latest announcement of sanctions, Mr Trump’s administration appears to have conceded its own limitations. History offers decades of evidence that economic sanctions alone do not force Iran to bend: if anything, they might strengthen the hands of the theocratic regime that has ruled Iran since 1979. In the days before the announcement, Mr Trump’s team had warned that countries that continue to trade with Iran or help it evade the effects of the sanctions would also face harsh penalties from the US, including secondary sanctions. However, thus far, the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has avoided imposing any such punishment on Iran’s trading partners to avoid sending the global financial system into a tailspin.

Implicit in that acknowledgement was a harsh fact: in a deeply-integrated global economy, any step the US takes to damage other countries will have adverse impacts on American consumers. The tariffs imposed by Mr Trump on most nations last year led to inflation in the US, and the war on Iran — resulting in oil price spikes — has raised the price tag of goods in American supermarkets. China, Iran’s largest economic ally, has made clear that it will not comply with US diktats. Russia will almost certainly ignore Mr Trump’s threats too. And they can afford to do so. Decades of economic warfare with the US have made China and Russia develop their financial structures independent of the US-led system. Consequently, the US can only impose limited additional damage to their economies. Generations of Iranians have weathered US sanctions as well. While many may not like their current rulers, they know that their economic crisis is an outcome — in good measure — of American policies. Like his predecessors, Mr Trump is unlikely to win against Iran with economic sanctions.

editorials.title: Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan worked
editorials.passage:
A pparently, he likes to say her name with a French accent . “Na-tah-lee!” the president cries out, in that affected tone of faux-formality that one might use with a person they love but do not quite respect, and she comes running, her thin legs teetering on her heels.

Natalie Harp , Trump’s 35-year-old “executive assistant”, was an odd recurring character in the latest blockbuster Trump administration book, Regime Change, by the New York Times’ Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. In the book, Harp features like a silent sentinel, ever present but eerily quiet as Trump rants and raves. It’s not exactly clear what the scope of her responsibilities are; though, as Jamelle Bouie points out, the fact that she evidently helps run the president’s social media accounts, which can sway markets and influence his foreign counterparts, makes her one of the most powerful people in the federal government.

But the dignity of Harp’s character does not often seem to equal the gravity of her influence: once, she was caught on video sprinting across a golf course on foot, chasing the golf cart that was speeding the president away to the next hole. For a while, she was called the “human printer” among Trump aides, in reference to the portable printer that Harp carries around with her: one of the primary ways she spends her time appears to be searching for flattering news stories and social media commentary about the president online, and printing it out to nourish his self-regard. But from Haberman and Swan’s reporting, it was not always clear exactly what Harp was thinking. Though many Trumpworld insiders are clearly identifiable as off-the-record sources in their book, Harp does not seem to be among them.

But recently, more of Harp’s own words have come to light. The Daily Beast published the full text of two letters from Harp to Trump, whose existence had previously been reported by Haberman and Swan. In the letters, Harp is rapturously worshipful, sycophantic, almost slavish. “You are all that matters to me,” she wrote to Trump. She called him her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”. (The capitalization is in the original.) It’s long been known that Trump prizes devotion among his underlings, that he seeks out flattering commentary about himself, and that he is surrounded, particularly in his second term, exclusively by the kind of people who will never tell him anything that he does not want to hear. Still, the spectacle of Harp’s obsequiousness – her willingness to debase herself for an 80-year-old man whose vulgarity, misogyny, racism, narcissism and impulsiveness have damaged her country in ways it will likely never recover from – is disturbing and grotesque.

Still, Harp herself might be less unsettling than the near certainty that there are others like her – White House staffers and federal bureaucrats and petty functionaries of the Maga machine – who have made flattery of Trump a large portion, if not the entirety, of their jobs. Likely, few Americans would ever have heard of Harp if it were not for Jon Ossoff, the Democratic Georgia senator running for re-election and widely assumed to be mulling a presidential bid, who mentioned Harp in a pointed barb in a campaign stump speech in Atlanta. Trump, Ossoff said , doesn’t want to do the job of president; he wants, instead, to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie”.

We do not need to be stupid: it strains credulity, and discredits the considerable savvy of Ossoff’s team, to claim that this remark was not meant to arouse salacious suspicion about the nature of Harp’s relationship with the president, and speculation that it might be sexual. Ossoff’s wording retained plausible deniability; still, I think he knew exactly what he was doing. Ossoff, in his campaign, has styled himself as firm-minded, resolute, and morally ambitious – an inheritor to Barack Obama . But in this remark, he diverged noticeably from Michelle Obama’s famous mantra “when they go low, we go high,” which has long been a shibboleth for the kind of Democratic politicians who have preferred dignity over effectiveness in the Trump era. Ossoff was going low.

It is shocking how well it worked. The evocation of Harp in Ossoff’s speech triggered a slew of news stories about the aide, delivered by White House reporters who seemed almost giddy to be able to cite as newsworthy something that before had been merely creepy. Asked about Harp on television, Haberman referred to her as Trump’s “binky” and “comfort blanket”, infantilizing him in humiliating terms. Trump surrogates were dispatched to defend Harp with a ferocity and insistence that couldn’t help but suggest that the president himself was angered. Ossoff, it seemed, had struck a nerve. At the beginning of Trump’s rise to power, many in politics gawked at his seemingly sui generis ability to dictate the news cycle: to say outrageous things, or make bizarre provocations, and send reporters, commentators, surrogates, and his opponents into a frenzy trying to respond to them. The effect was that Trump determined the subject of discourse; everyone else responded to him. Ossoff turned the tables, and he made it look easy.

One of the allegations that Trump’s aides spewed in their responses to the remark was that in insinuating that something inappropriate was afoot between Trump and Harp, Ossoff was being sexist. Those on the left rushed to discount this: no one, after all, really believes that Donald Trump , he of “grab ’em by the pussy”, is leading a movement that has serious or sincere concerns for women’s dignity. But to say that Ossoff’s remark contained no misogyny would be naive, if not dishonest: if his suggestion was made deliberately, then he was using Harp’s gender to undermine her professionalism, and to evoke a sex scandal. Of course there is misogyny in this gesture, the suggestion that a young woman is not entirely serious. That Harp’s character and conduct suggest this much more than her sex does need not force us to pretend not to see things that we do.

What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark? For my part, I do not see any equivalence between the misogyny imposed on American women by the Trump regime – or, for that matter, the misogyny imposed on American women by Trump personally – and the minor distastefulness of Ossoff. It’s like comparing a dropper of water to the Pacific Ocean. Every woman, every feminist, knows that she has accepted things out of necessity or convenience that the most stringent adherence to principle would require her to reject. And I confess, I am more encouraged by Ossoff’s pugnaciousness than I am put off by the gendered undertones of the remark. After all, it is a grim reality of our gendered world that wherever there is a straight man who esteems himself to be godlike and extraordinary, there will be a straight woman somewhere not far behind who inexplicably believes him. We must work on building a world where this is not true. The first step might be getting this guy out of the White House.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

editorials.title: We surveyed 6,000 Americans. Here is the winning message for Democrats
editorials.passage:
T his year’s Democratic primaries look and sound a lot more populist than usual. Brian Poindexter , a union iron worker running on a “workers first” message, won a House primary outside Cleveland. Sherrod Brown is mounting a Senate comeback in Ohio on the same “rigged system” message that has allowed him to outshine other Democrats in Ohio. Troy Jackson , a fifth-generation logger who built his career fighting corporate landowners, is the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine. And Josh Turek , a self-described “prairie populist”, is on the Senate ballot in Iowa.

In fact, according to research we’ve conducted through the Center for Working-Class Politics (CWCP), more than 70% of 2026 Democratic candidates now rely on populist rhetoric in their campaigns, laying the blame for our broken system on rich elites of one kind or another.

It seems after decades of bleeding working-class support, Democrats are converging on a solution to win them back: run populists.

The real question, then, is not whether Democrats should embrace populism, but rather what kind of populism they should embrace. To settle that argument, CWCP teamed up with the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative (RUBI) to conduct a new survey .

In polling fielded by Verasight between late June and early July, we asked more than 6,000 Americans to rate 13 different kinds of messages commonly deployed by Democratic candidates to see which pitch would draw the strongest support. We also randomly presented each respondent with one of two Republican attack messages modeled on actual Republican campaign rhetoric in order to see how well Democratic messages hold up under attack.

The top-performing messages we tested have a simple formula. They focus on Americans’ day-to-day struggles to pay for rent and groceries, and the widespread frustration with prices that rise faster than working-class wages. They insist that working people should be able to give their kids a better shot. They promise to bring costs down, make the biggest corporations pay their fair share, and crack down on the people who game the system. Ultimately, they tell a simple story: hard work should pay off.

We call this winning combination “kitchen-table populism”.

None of the plausible alternatives to this kind of messaging performed nearly as well. Consider what we call the “divide-and-conquer playbook” messaging popular with certain progressive campaign consultants. One prominent proponent of this style is the Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico. Talarico strikes a populist posture, emphasizing that economic elites keep working people divided over race, immigration, and cultural issues so that no one sees that they’re all getting fleeced. It sounds good, and Talarico is holding his own in red Texas, but this tactic is not the slam dunk against the culture war that some progressives think it is. In fact, in our survey, it was not all that effective, severely underperforming the pure kitchen-table messages we tested.

The weakest variant of the divide-and-conquer narrative is the one that tells voters they’ve been tricked into blaming scapegoats. These “race-class narrative” appeals, so popular in progressives circles, finished at the bottom of the field. Why? Because telling people they’ve been duped comes off more like a condescending sermon than an invitation. Unlike kitchen-table populist messages that meet voters where they’re at, the race-class narrative strays from voters’ concrete economic woes to expound a more abstract theory of political gamesmanship. These messages trailed our top kitchen-table populist pitches with every group, including non-white voters and Democrats.

Another alternative to populist messaging is a big-tent anti-Trumpism, pushed by some establishment liberals. The argument here is that candidates could unite all those Never-Trump Republicans, anti-Trump independents, and Resistance Democrats with a simple opposition message – one that steers clear of divisions over policy or ideology. Again, the theory makes sense. The trouble is that messaging focused on attacking Trump performed poorly across the board. We fielded the strongest-testing anti-Trump message we know, one that ties his attacks on democratic norms directly to pocketbook pain, and even this steelman version was a net negative with rural voters and Trump waverers.

It wasn’t all roses for populism either. We found that anti-elite messages varied in their efficacy. While naming corruption, and promising to end it, was a powerful way to convey anti-elite sentiments – especially with Republicans, where adding an anti-corruption pledge to a plain cost-of-living pitch lifted support by 18 points – messages that leaned too stridently into class war turned off these same voters. Republicans swung 25 points against messages that blamed “big corporations” and “the wealthy few.”

We also tested a progressive-coded anti-plutocrat message that railed against oligarchs and fascists: it trailed kitchen-table populism by about 14 points among Democrats and by huge margins among working-class, rural, and swing voters.

To be clear, this shouldn’t be understood as a plea for centrism or moderation. While it may seem like Democratic candidates are forced into a trade-off – either you opt to fire up the progressive base with ultra-liberal anti-Trump bromides or you aim to persuade Trump-voting working-class voters with a more conservative pitch – our results show that this is a false choice. The winning messages do neither; instead, they name a rigged system, call out the people rigging it, and promise to rebalance the economy in favor of those who work for a living. But they also avoid moral high-handedness and the preachy activist rhetoric that turns off many working class, rural, and swing voters. These are the lessons Democrats must internalize if they want to win back the working class, including some of the 59% of working-class white voters who, according to a March poll by Catalist, still plan to vote Republican in 2026.

Some of the strongest-performing Democrats have already shown the power of kitchen-table populism in tough districts. Pat Ryan rode what he calls “patriotic populism” to a 14-point win in a Hudson Valley swing district in 2024, naming greedy corporations and corrupt politicians as the villains while casting working people as heroes. And Gabe Vasquez has won one of the country’s toughest seats in rural New Mexico two times with a similar pitch: Vasquez points the finger at corporate landlords, elites in Washington DC, and price-gouging investors who get rich by bending the rules, while praising hard-working blue-collar families that are struggling to stay afloat. That’s the winning formula, one we hope to see more Democrats and independents deploy.

Dustin “Dino” Guastella is director of operations for Teamsters Local 623 in Philadelphia and sits on the board of the Center for Working-Class Politics

Erica Etelson is president of the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative

editorials.title: If MPs want to take on Nigel Farage over his dodgy finances, they need to clean up their own act
editorials.passage:
H ow has your summer been? Done anything nice? As MPs prepare to head back to parliament next week, you’ll be relieved to hear that some of the most prominent figures in British politics have been enjoying the season’s cultural highlights – and without paying a penny. MPs throughout the Commons have received £400,000 of “freebies” to concerts, sports matches and other events so far this year, according to the most recent disclosures.

Over the summer alone, Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, enjoyed the Chelsea flower show thanks to Lloyds Banking Group covering the £1,839 cost, as did the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride. Lucy Powell, who has since become deputy leader of the Labour party and education secretary, accepted £858-worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group. Meanwhile, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, nabbed seats at Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the All England Club.

Totalled up, MPs have been gifted £100,000 more so far this year than in the whole of 2025, with recipients seemingly learning few lessons from Keir Starmer’s “passes for glasses” scandal , in which a Labour peer gifted the then prime minister designer eyewear and clothes before being spotted in Downing Street with a temporary security pass.

Like many of these types of stories, there’s some nuance lurking behind the headlines. MPs quite rightly go to events linked to their constituency or local area. Andy Burnham accepting £3,800 tickets to the Brit awards in Manchester – when he was the regional mayor – to spotlight the city hosting the event for the first time is not the same as Streeting presumably just really wanting to meet Monty Don.

The increase can also partly be explained by the fact MPs have become more consistent about declaring hospitality on the parliamentary register after Starmer changed the rules, while ticket prices are well known to have gone up across the board. And yet, wade through the details of gigs and horse racing and it’s hard not to conclude some MPs are simply practising blatant grifting. Call it a treat for a seat, where our elected officials are enjoying must-see shows as a kind of unofficial bonus.

That much of this stuff was gifted by big business, including gambling firms and banks, makes the whole thing feel considerably grubbier. Why did the betting company Flutter want to shower then local backbencher and now chief whip, Anneliese Midgley, with high-priced tickets to the Grand National and Cheltenham?

Public perception of such luxury perks will be even more unforgiving against a backdrop of an ongoing cost of living crisis. A night at the Ivor Novello awards may not be the duck house-level opulence of 2009’s expenses scandal , but the optics are little better. While much of the population are struggling to pay their electric and food bills, MPs are getting out the fascinators for Ladies’ Day at Aintree.

Politicians, of course, are human. Who among us wouldn’t be tempted by Harry Styles? The electorate, for its part, tends to want leaders to connect with everyday life. There’s a reason why Malcolm Tucker in The Thick of It – based on the rumour Alastair Campbell got Tony Blair clips of EastEnders and reality shows – makes a “ zeitgeist tape ” to help his useless ministers seem “in touch”. But it would be disingenuous to pretend MPs are driven to accept hospitality gifts as a bid to be down to earth , or that balancing such demands from the public is somehow a complex, grey area. Most people like to see their MP letting loose at a concert – they just want them to have paid for their ticket.

With the standards watchdog due to question Nigel Farage when parliament reopens – an inquiry he temporarily dodged by calling a byelection – the coming weeks will very likely see a renewed focus on what MPs receive and the transparency around it.

On paper, Farage’s gifts are in another league to his colleagues’ freebies: forget a ticket to the tennis, we’re talking £5m from a crypto billionaire and further “financial support” from a convicted fraudster . And yet to a public who have for decades seen front-page stories about politicians’ finances – from expenses and second jobs to tax avoidance – the idea that the Reform UK leader is an outlier worth investigating rather than one of a bad bunch can feel at best a hard sell and, at worst, hypocritical.

If MPs wish to be able to hold Farage to account with credibility, they will need to show they care about cash and transparency in every form. That means the government looking harder into how some MPs are using their influence to make extra money, not least when it’s linked with the growth of the far right. Just this week it emerged that the Restore leader, Rupert Lowe, is set to earn as much from his – anti-migrant – posts on X as he does from his MP’s salary (which he gives to charity) since Elon Musk took over and financially rewarded some high-reach posts. “Gifts” come in many forms.

Winning public trust will also require MPs to be squeaky-clean themselves and stop accepting hospitality unless it’s linked to their constituency – even if that means watching the Chelsea flower show on iPlayer like the rest of us.

Because every time an MP goes to an event for free, it comes with a hidden cost: a public with ever-decreasing faith in the political class, who are more likely to greet outright corruption or cronyism with a weary shrug. “They’re all the same” is a dangerous public mood for a democracy and one that, once embedded, can be deeply hard to dislodge.

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Food allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planes
editorials.passage:
W hat are you most scared of? Perhaps snakes send a chill down your spine. Or heights leave your knees weak. Peanuts may sound like an odd source of phobia, but they have taken on an absurd bogeyman quality for me since my daughter was taken to hospital by ambulance after eating peanut butter when she was six months old. Just the sight of a bowl on a pub bar, or their shells discarded on the pavement, can raise my heart rate – even when I’m not with her.

Nowhere is the sight of peanuts more confronting than at 30,000ft, especially now when millions are jetting back from their holidays. Travelling with a severely allergic child can be a nightmare for all sorts of reasons, but the idea you could be sat next to a passenger consuming the very thing that has hospitalised them is its own kind of hell.

Most airlines will make an announcement asking passengers to avoid consuming nuts if you let them know that somebody in your party has a severe nut allergy. But I brace for impact when these announcements are piped out. On almost every flight there is at least one passenger who sighs or makes some inane comment, loud enough for everyone to hear, about how annoying it is.

Oh, I’m sorry – is not being able to eat nuts for a few hours inconveniencing you? Does one passenger’s desire to consume peanut M&M’s trump someone else’s right to stay alive? I didn’t realise the right to eat nuts was a civil liberties issue. How utterly absurd.

And yet, people get disproportionately upset about being told not to eat things. Chloë Dickson, who runs the Instagram account peanutfreezone, recently posted a horrifying video of her experience flying with a severe peanut allergy and a man behind her responding, “Really?” to an announcement asking passengers not to eat nuts. He “then proceeded to make comments throughout the entire journey about eating peanuts around me, along with two other people nearby,” the caption reads.

I am mystified by this mean-spiritedness. Allergies are not a lifestyle choice but a medical condition. And yet, they seem to inspire a lack of empathy in the public consciousness. Perhaps it’s due to a misunderstanding of what allergy actually is. For people such as Chloe and my daughter, we’re not talking about skin irritation or a dodgy stomach, however unpleasant that might be. Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can affect multiple body systems and commonly impacts breathing or consciousness. The primary treatment is adrenaline via an EpiPen and it requires immediate medical attention.

But I suspect many people do know what severe allergy can look like, they just think this level of caution is overblown and are frustrated by having to make accommodations. Take a look at some of the comments under Chloë’s post and you’ll see what I mean. They are staggering in their stupidity. “Fly private or DON’T FLY AT ALL. Don’t make other people’s lives miserable just to please yours!” one reads. “I travel with a bag of peanuts for these moments,” says another. There really are people who seem to believe that those with allergies should just not travel at all. Or not go out to eat. Or not be able to participate fully in life outside their own homes. I wonder if they would feel that way if it was their children who were diagnosed.

Allergic people can’t be wrapped in cotton wool. Some of the best advice I got when my daughter was small, from an angelic NHS allergy nurse, was that you do your very best to keep her safe and then you carry EpiPens as your insurance policy. That’s given me lots of comfort over the years when gauging risk. But when you’re trapped in a metal tube in the sky with no possibility of medical attention, the stakes feel much higher.

What scares allergic people most is not necessarily the risk of an airborne reaction, which is vanishingly rare , it’s the possibility of cross-contamination. That peanut dust on someone’s fingers could then spread to the tray table, the seat, perhaps the toilet door. That a rogue peanut from a previous flight has fallen between the seats or touched the seatbelt. On quick turnaround budget airlines with minimal cleaning, the risk you may come into contact with the allergen starts to feel frighteningly high. And even tiny amounts of nut protein can trigger a life-threatening reaction for some people.

Banning nuts on planes seems like a no-brainer. And I say nuts because of all the common allergens, they are the least likely to be outgrown in childhood and have a higher rate of causing severe reactions . That means telling passengers not to bring nut products on board. But even just stopping the practice of serving them on flights would drastically reduce the risk of cross-contamination when travelling. And it would take the pressure off anxious, allergic passengers to advocate for their safety. Of course, no ban could be watertight, which is why airlines should make a blanket rule that anyone with severe allergy should be offered priority boarding to clean their own seats before takeoff as a precaution.

Allergic people shouldn’t have to justify their medical needs to people who don’t understand them. Banning nuts on planes could send an important message to the broader public. That people with allergies should be able to travel without fear. That compassionate societies make accommodations.

Lucy Pasha-Robinson is a Guardian assistant Opinion editor

editorials.title: It’s time for all of us to get a grip and stop flaking on friends for no good reason
editorials.passage:
I t’s a Thursday night. You are sitting on the couch (the TV is on or you could be reading a book but most likely you are doom-scrolling). You know full well that you have plans to meet a dear friend who you’ve been “meaning to catch up with for ages!” at the pub down the road in exactly 45 minutes.

Maybe this friend has been going through a rough time? Maybe they’ve got some exciting news about a perfect Hinge date (rare and shocking)? Maybe you’ve simply been “ships in the night” sailing through the capitalist rat race and miss each other’s company.

Either way, this hangout is premeditated and has been organised in advance with many exclamations of excitement. However, there is but one tiny problem: you no longer want to go. You are just … comfortable where you are.

You vaguely start calculating the hours left in the day – you might want to go to the gym in the morning (despite not having gone in weeks) and work was slightly strenuous today (you had to actually do your job).

You pick up your phone to text them something along the lines of “Massive day today – can we postpone? Maybe the weekend after next? Don’t wanna have a big one on a school night!” None of this is due to any sort of change of heart towards your pal: you simply can’t be bothered.

I think the most alarming thing about this scenario is how real it is. It’s been me. It’s been you. It might even be you right now, reading this article.

The swing into prioritising self care over endless hustle has swung too far and now it is completely normal to cancel on one another because we are desperate to avoid even the most minor discomfort, ie going out in public and down the road for a perfect glass of wine. Using the excuse of “it’s a school night” feels particularly sinister coming from a (usually) millennial or gen Z who hasn’t attended school in over a decade.

The self-infantilisation must cease immediately!

On a personal note, I’ve spent the last year firmly reacquainting with my personal capability. I am extremely capable! And actually … we all are. I now lie in bed at night, grinding my molars to nubs, vowing to stop any and all weak behaviours. Being unable, as a fully functioning adult with the gift of a healthy body and mind, to get up off the couch for no reason other than “cbf” is weak. You will catch me muttering to myself “being uncomfortable is not the same as being unsafe”. Life is precious and living is a verb. Insufferable? Sure! But! I don’t think I’m wrong.

We have become addicted to comfort – we can order anything direct to the door, we “connect” with others through our phones, we are entertained by TikTok and Netflix and endless gaming options. We can live our lives in the hikikomori style – without ever having to engage with another human person. My feed is clogged with videos of skinny people glamorising “protecting your peace”, “self-dating” and doing expensive morning and evening routines (alone). I’m constantly besieged by muted infographics encouraging me to lean into my “soft girl era” which really feels like … laziness repackaged.

The insipid emphasis on seclusion is far too normalised. Humans are social.

We need our friends and our communities more than ever. We need to feel real connection and prioritise our actual relationships over a 30-second video from someone we will never meet. “Popping over for a chat” is almost a lost art. In this digital age, with the horrifying tendrils of AI draining our water reservoirs, poised to topple entire creative industries, getting in a room together feels unfortunately more and more radical by the year.

So, if you’ve said you’re gonna do something with a mate – do it.

News flash: the world is a hot mess right now and no one really wants to do anything. We’ve all got full calendars. Say no upfront! Being with our friends IRL is a joy and a treat not a chore, and energy actually begets more energy (one thing the fitness girls are right about). It’s time to collectively get a grip. Go out and have some fun – I promise it’s always better than staying on the couch.

Johanna Cosgrove is an award-winning actor/writer/comedian

editorials.title: A Britain of wildfires and flood risks: be sure, the climate crisis is real, and we will deal with it
editorials.passage:
T his long, hot summer has brought our third drought in five years and the driest July in almost two centuries . We’ve seen wildfires burn down homes and now face the risk of flash floods as we move into autumn. It should be a wake-up call for those saying that concerns about the climate crisis are overblown; that we should simply sit back and do nothing; or row back on attempts to restore our natural environment. As the new environment secretary, I won’t let that happen.

No one who has experienced this summer in the UK should be in any doubt that our climate is already changing. We know the future holds warmer, wetter winters, hotter, drier summers, and more extreme weather.

Honesty about what is required to deal with this changing reality is the least we should expect from our politicians. But last week we saw an astonishing response from Reform UK’s deputy leader, who told people to “enjoy” the scorching heatwaves and described this government’s efforts to combat the climate crisis as “arrogant”.

This response isn’t just ignorant; it is insulting.

Insulting to the firefighters risking their lives to fight blazes up and down the country. Insulting to the public whose lives are disrupted by scorching temperatures that were once a rare occurrence. And insulting to our farmers struggling to turn a profit as drought damages their crops.

This government’s response is not to throw in the towel and accept the chaos caused by extreme weather. It is to work to build and manage landscapes so they are resilient enough to withstand it and recover.

We know that healthy ecosystems retain more water and can help act as natural firebreaks. That resilience does not just protect us from the impacts of wildfire. It guards against flooding and pollution, too.

But some, including the Conservatives, have made the argument that rewilding lowers resilience to fire and that we should reverse restrictions on burning heather on our moors and peatlands. The exact opposite is true.

The evidence clearly shows that wetter, healthy peatlands hold more water and are less likely to develop species that are vulnerable to fires. The damage that has been done to these vital habitats by decades of burning has made them more vulnerable to wildfires in the long term, not less.

The solution to raging wildfires is not more burning of our countryside. It is to restore and better manage our environment.

Where rewilding has been prioritised , as at the National Trust’s Holnicote estate, you can clearly see the stark difference that it makes to the ability to withstand extreme weather. In areas where rivers and wetlands have been restored, the plants are green and blooming. Elsewhere, the ground is brown and dry.

As environment secretary, most of what comes across my desk is underpinned by the need to adapt to our changing climate – and this government is taking these challenges head on.

That’s why the prime minister this month convened an emergency Cobra meeting , bringing together senior ministers, firefighters, weather forecasters and other experts to make sure we’re doing all we can to keep the country safe from wildfires. That includes a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues.

We are spending almost £100m to strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to wildfires and extreme weather.

And we are backing our farmers during the drought with a £65m funding boost , rule changes to make building on-site reservoirs easier and the largest nature-friendly budget in history to make our farms more resilient to extreme weather and to protect our food security.

Adapting to our changing climate demands sustained attention, effort and investment. Others may simply deny the problem or stick their heads in the sand, but this government will rise to the challenge.

Angela Eagle is the secretary of state for environment, food and rural affairs

editorials.title: A new book looks at the history of the sari and all that it supports socially and economically
editorials.passage:
The deep involvement and complete sense of identity of the Indian woman with the sari, has made her resist the pressure to change her style of dress, inadvertently providing continuity in weaving traditions of every part of the country. The sari represents a culture in which the woven and textured-with-pattern garment; unpierced or intruded upon by the stitching needle; was considered not only more appropriate in terms of aesthetics and climate, but was also an act of greater purity and simplicity. It is difficult to historically ascertain the sari’s evolution as a single piece drape, though in many parts of India (Kerala, the six northeast states, Rajasthan and Gujarat), its possible preceding versions of two or three-piece drapes, continue to be worn.

The sari allows us to go back at least a thousand years in terms of design. It is conceived on the loom as a three-dimensional garment with variables in pattern, weave and structure between its inner and outer end-pieces and its two borders, which provide drape, strength and weight, while the body enhances its drape. All these elements help maintain the form of the sari when it is worn.

A process of awareness began with the Master Weavers Exhibition in 1982 and continued through a series of seven Visvakarma exhibitions, initiated by Martand Singh and supported by the Development Commissioner (Handlooms), Government of India, attempting to discover whether a level of excellence was still possible in the tradition of handcrafted textiles. It led to the recognition of a handful of craftsmen in different parts of the country, who were still capable of giving us a glimpse of the best of their inherited skills. They gave us the confidence to move beyond the museum masterpieces, to look for what could be achieved today. Though the experience of searching, finding and attempting to revitalise within a contemporary context was exhilarating in itself, it left one with a feeling of standing on thin ice. How little we know about the craftsman, his capabilities and the dire circumstances out of which “design” emerges. What exactly is possible within a specific area of skill? How can the range of handloom weaving, printing and dyeing be developed further without adequate knowledge of its specific capabilities, capacities, potential strength and limitations? This growing awareness and the realisation that too much had already been allowed to die out of sheer neglect, combined with a final assault by power looms and mills during the second half of the 20th century, brought a sense of urgency to this documentation project.

In more ancient times, weavers were taken from one kingdom to another as part of a dowry in marriage, or given as the price of conquest. At less fortunate times, they were conscripted as soldiers or were forced to migrate due to oppression, want, or famine. They carried the sapling of knowledge wherever they went, adding to the wealth of their newfound homeland.

The sari has been a unifying feature, despite the variations in its wearing style, in different parts of India. The urban wearing style is a post-1870s phenomenon and is described as follows in Chitra Debi’s marvellous book from the 1970s, Thakur Barir Onder Mohal (translated from Bengali by Riten Mazumdar):

It is said that Satyendranath (elder brother of Rabindranath) Tagore’s wife, Gyanodanandini, went with her civil servant husband to Bombay around the 1870s and adopted the Parsi way of wearing the sari, as at that time the local Bengali way was not considered elegant enough for outdoor wear. On her return to Calcutta we find that this style, now known in the Thakur Barir as the Bombay Dastur, was adopted by all the ladies of the Barir and other society ladies referred to it as the “Thakur Barir Sari”. In fact, when Gyanoda advertised her willingness to teach this style of wearing the sari – with a saya or petticoat, chemise blouse and jacket – it attracted a number of women. It seems to have been a time when a number of ladies were experimenting with supposedly more sophisticated ways of wearing the sari. The sari went through various stages of resembling the hobble skirt and the gown. At one stage the pallav (end-piece) was made so short that it could not cover the head and thus, a mukut (crown/tiara) was worn with a flowing backcloth. Suniti Devi, the Maharani of Cooch Behar, preferred to have a scarf over the head, worn like a Spanish mantilla. Eventually, the traditional way seemed to make a comeback with some alteration in the early twentieth century, for the pallav was brought back over the head by Gyanoda’s daughter, Indira Devi. We find that Suniti Devi’s sister Sucharu Devi, Maharani of Mayurbhanj, was seen at the Delhi Darbar in 1903 in this modern style of wearing the sari, though she said that this was her in-laws’ way of wearing it. Bengali ladies seem to have adopted this more convenient way, though they kept Gyanoda’s way of taking the pallav over the left shoulder.

Although it is a fast-disappearing garment for everyday wear, the sari will survive as special occasion wear. More and more Indian women today prefer stitched garments and Western wear of easy-to-maintain and wash-and-wear fabrics. And yet, there was a time when they rode horses wearing saris in Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh and even swam in rivers and ponds with their sari tucked between the legs, much like an unstitched pair of shorts. Saris were even draped longer in pantaloon-like fashion, in places as far apart as Shajapur, Madhya Pradesh and Kothapalli in Andhra Pradesh. If the principles of these wearing styles were put into practice, many more could possibly be evolved for contemporary needs. Interestingly, the sari is asserting a growing presence in the boardrooms of multinational corporate organisations, in law chambers, courts, and among the new power professionals who are conscious of their identity and wish to draw strength from it.

In the contemporary context, despite the growing compulsion to industrialise and globalise, there is also an increasing awareness of ecological viability and sound growth. With her rich resources of skilled hand-spinning and weaving, India is advantageously placed to show the way in balancing the slower but high-skilled production sectors with the mechanised, high-technology end. Though there has been a gradual exodus from these professions in the 20th century, what they are going through today is unprecedented. Weavers are losing a high-skill livelihood without alternative options, facing starvation-like conditions and joining the ranks of the unskilled.

The sari is not only known by different names (lugda, dhoti, pata, seere, sadlo, kapad) in various parts of the country, but is also conceived differently in form and structure, in usage and custom. It is a stretch of fabric, long or short, wide or narrow – according to who wears it and the way in which it is worn. There is, in fact, no “one type of sari”.

Despite 108 variations of the sari drape and wearing style being featured in this book, a personal variant is always possible. This distinguishes the sari as the most unique and versatile of garments. In constant play with the body, in stillness and in movement, allowing for adjustments at all times. Be it the vigour of working in the fields or squatting on the kitchen floor, it transforms itself according to need and function. In the manner of her carrying the sari, the wearer reveals her nature and demeanour. The bold and the shy, the silent but inquisitive, the athletic yet graceful – all manner of women hold their saris with characteristic ease, almost as if it were their second skin rather than a textile extraneous to themselves.

The personal pleasure of draping the unstitched, fluid garment over and around the body, adjusting it with little tucks and pulls to suit one’s own particular form, is sensuous. It creates a picture of flowing grace that conceals as much as it reveals.

This book has emerged from travel-based research conducted over three and a half months in each of the states described, except Goa and Kerala. Each state was initially mapped out according to weaver/printer settlements and products from gazettes and other records that went back a hundred years. The states were covered by my colleague Amba Sanyal and me, together or with the respective research team in the states. We travelled with the teams, at least for the initial six to eight districts, keeping diaries and swapping them with team members every night, just as we had kept them on our very first tour in 1984. The period of field travel was primarily from 1984 to 1991, though Andhra Pradesh was completed in 1997, and I had to undertake verification tours in 2002-03. We were looking out for what was traditionally woven in the area on the scale of living memory, and exploring design directories and fabric structures with the oldest weavers, in large gatherings of thirty to sixty weavers in each village. This helped initiate our researchers into the hectic process of listening, discussing, writing, travelling and photographing; at the pace of two to three villages, ten to 12 hours, traversing approximately 100 kilometres each day. Working on this project has been a rewarding experience, even though it has meant much more work for us, with the teams having spent over a year or more putting together the material on each state.

When we first started our travel, the search for the who, what, why and how of the traditional design directory focused on the main production and trade centres of each state. During the first three months on the road, we realised that the clues and inspiration for several well-known textiles lay in lesser-known areas. It was a classic case of “one place leading to another”. Before we knew it, we were following the trail of weaver/printer/dyer settlements village by village, in almost every district of the state.

We did not expect to find so much evidence of what lay beneath the surface of the pyramid, let alone meet weavers who had seen or woven the textiles that made up the grand symphony of the handloom tradition in India. Many were persuaded to weave them once again and we were soon embroiled in the production and post-production problems of the textiles themselves, rather than the documentation. Looking into their marketability today… Were they good enough? How do we develop design directories for each area? These were the questions before us. Weavers commonly said, “What use is the book to us now, when we need to make a living?” However, they conceded that it would be useful to them in the long run.

The sari has been our means of finding a pathway through the labyrinth of India’s inherited material/ textile culture. The most fluid of worn garments, the sari reflects and communicates with all that we can see and touch, feel and experience. It takes us headlong into the intangible aesthetic, philosophy and technology from which it emerges. It is our roadmap for Bharat darshan – a visitation of this land. Often enough, the underlying linkages are not fully perceived as they are too far removed from the overwhelming reality of the present in which they exist. Yet, as this is not a historical account but one based on living memory, it is the practitioners who provide the clues, however faint, through colour and material associations, names and meanings of symbolic patterns and usage of particular saris. In retrospect, the sari’s significance becomes clearer.

Excerpted with permission from Saris: Tradition and Beyond, Rta Kapur Chishti, Roli Books.

editorials.title: Is Census 2027 the first step to a National Register of Citizens?
editorials.passage:
The list of questions for the 2027 census has stoked fears that census data might be used to prepare a National Register of Citizens.

The questionnaire for the 2027 census includes 12 questions that were not asked in the previous census. Ten of these were part of the contentious National Population Register that the Modi government had attempted to conduct in 2020.

With these inclusions, the census has subsumed the National Population Register, which is the first step towards drawing up a National Register of Citizens.

Scroll spoke to lawyers, activists and politicians to understand what the collapse of the distinction between the census and the National Population Register means. Most were of the view that this move could trigger anxieties about citizenship similar to those that had sparked the nationwide protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019.

The main purpose of the census is to collect statistical data about India’s population and their housing and social conditions. But the 2027 census will go beyond questions that allow administrators to construct a statistical picture of how Indians live.

It will, for instance, ask respondents where and when their parents were born and which religion they practiced. Activists worry that this could set off a cycle of investigations and inquiries into the citizenship of those who have been living in India for generations, especially if they are Muslims.

The population enumeration phase of the census, during which enumerators go door-to-door with a questionnaire, will begin in snowbound parts of North India in September. At least 12 of the 40 questions to be asked as part of this process have never been asked in a census before. These include details about a respondent’s spouse, parentage, nationality and identification documents, such as passport, Aadhaar and voter card number.

This information was meant to be collected in 2020 as part of the National Population Register but the exercise had to be shelved back then on account of the Covid-19 pandemic. However, even before the pandemic, the National Population Register had been met with fierce opposition from civil society groups because of its design.

Specifically, questions about where and when a respondent’s parents were born caused concern as these could, in theory, help determine whether they were Indian citizens. A 2003 amendment to the Citizenship Act made the citizenship of those born in India after June 30, 1987, contingent on the citizenship of their parents.

Those controversial questions have now been included in the census as “father’s particulars” and “mother’s particulars”. Scroll accessed the training manual meant for government officials involved in conducting the exercise to find out what these “particulars” entail. They include name, date of birth, place of birth and religion.

Census enumerators were already expected to ask respondents for their name, date of birth, place of birth and religion. Now, they will have to obtain these details for every respondent’s parents too, raising fears that the data could be used to create a National Register of Citizens.

“NPR combined with NRC and CAA was what we were really fearing in 2019,” said human rights activist Harsh Mander. “The whole agitation at that time was against this. One hoped that the government would have learned lessons from it and set aside this project. But just the first glance at the census seems to suggest that they are going the whole way.”

The National Population Register flows from the sweeping changes that the Atal Bihari Vajpayee-led National Democratic Alliance government made in India’s citizenship law in 2003. This included defining, for the first time, who an “illegal migrant” was. It then introduced the Citizenship Rules to implement these changes on the ground through, among other things, the National Population Register.

The first National Population Register was consequently drawn up in 2010 and then updated in 2015. The database reportedly contains information about 119 crore residents of the country. All of this data was collected by the same body that conducts the census: the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India.

However, in 2020, the National Population Register became mired in controversy for two reasons. First, the National Register of Citizens exercise in Assam caused chaos by excluding over 19 lakh people from the final list. The majority of them were Hindus.

And second, the Bharatiya Janata Party promised to create a nationwide National Register of Citizens – that it linked to religion through the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019. Now, by subsuming the National Population Register into the census, the Modi government risks reviving the controversy.

“There is a grave danger that the census is becoming an instrument not of collecting information but of finding grounds to exclude and expel targeted communities, especially Muslims, from citizenship,” Mander said.

Legally, the process of storing and using data collected for the National Population Register is very different from the census. The latter has strong protections in place. “No person shall have a right to inspect any book, register or record made by a census officer in the discharge of his duty,” reads section 15 of the Census Act, 1948 .

In contrast, the National Population Register database can be shared with other departments of the Union government as well as state governments. In fact, the 2003 rules say that the National Register of Citizens has to be prepared after verifying entries in the National Population Register.
